selected_subject.role: Anchorage Assembly Member (Eagle River / Chugiak district)
selected_subject.anchorage_tie: Elected member of the Anchorage Assembly representing the Eagle River/Chugiak district within the Municipality of Anchorage; the decision governs an APD surveillance-analytics system (Real-Time Crime Center) deployed across the Anchorage bowl.

subject_quotes.verbatim: All the guardrails that you just stated are policy and when my constituents ask, 'what are we collecting? Who can see it? How long do we keep it?' Anchorage code can't answer any of those questions
subject_quotes.context: McCormick objecting, at the Aug 4 2026 Assembly meeting, that the RTCC upgrade's oversight rests only on executive-branch policy rather than binding municipal code.

subject_quotes.verbatim: We have no legislative guardrails. This is an entirely bundling power under the executive branch without any check or balance.
subject_quotes.context: McCormick arguing the RTCC contract concentrates surveillance authority in the executive branch absent code-level checks.

selected_decision.what_happened: At the August 4, 2026 Anchorage Assembly meeting, members declined to approve APD's proposed ~$600,000 three-year contract with Thundercat Technology Inc. to upgrade the Real-Time Crime Center and postponed action to the August 18, 2026 meeting, with McCormick leading the objection that the municipality has no code-level data-governance rules over what the RTCC collects, who can access it, and how long it is retained.

corroborating_sources.outlet: MOA Public Health and Safety Committee packet

selected_decision.the_binary: Fund the ~$600k three-year Thundercat RTCC analytics upgrade now, versus withhold approval until Anchorage Municipal Code sets binding collection/access/retention guardrails.
selected_decision.ak_consequence: Municipal algorithmic-surveillance sector: the fate of APD's ~$600,000 three-year Thundercat contract for an RTCC that ingests up to 750 camera feeds plus drones, license-plate readers, and object-recognition analytics, and whether Anchorage adopts code-level data-governance guardrails, is decided at the August 18, 2026 Assembly vote, directly affecting APD, Thundercat, and every Anchorage resident subject to the system.
selected_decision.debatable_axis: Pro: withholding approval forces democratic, code-level guardrails onto an expanding object-recognition/ALPR surveillance apparatus before it is entrenched. Con: the delay stalls public-safety tooling APD says it needs, and the 2023 facial-recognition ban plus the chief's committee-notification commitments may already supply workable oversight without holding the contract hostage.

structural_read: This is a genuine governance decision at the exact seam Alaska AI oversight tends to fall through: the object of the contract is not an 'AI model' but the algorithmic-analytics and camera/ALPR/drone infrastructure that surveillance AI runs on, and McCormick's objection is squarely about the missing legal architecture, collection scope, access, retention, rather than the technology's merits. That framing is credible and load-bearing: Anchorage barred facial recognition in 2023 but, on this record, has no binding code governing the object-recognition and Flock-style analytics the RTCC upgrade would expand. The weakness in the file is corroboration depth, not substance: the specific postponement-and-objection is carried in detail by a single independent outlet (Alaska's News Source), with MOA's own documents and a Must Read Alaska legislative-priorities piece confirming the RTCC's scale (up to 750 feeds, a stated $1.5M municipal ask) but not independently reconstructing the Aug 4 debate. The countervailing case is real, APD frames this as routine public-safety modernization, and a reasonable member could vote to approve with committee notification as the check, which is why it clears the position-takeable bar rather than reading as advocacy.
forward_implication: The binding vote lands at the August 18, 2026 Assembly meeting. Watch whether McCormick converts his objection into a code-level data-governance amendment (collection/access/retention rules) as a condition of approval, or whether the Assembly approves the Thundercat contract as-is and defers governance to executive-branch policy. His prior 'no' on the March 2026 data-center zoning ordinance AO 2026-27 suggests he will keep pressing the guardrails-before-infrastructure line.
